segments.narration: Someone chiselled a pharaoh off her own temple walls. Hatshepsut ruled Egypt for about twenty-one years, carved in stone wearing the false beard of a king.
She left the terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari and twin obelisks at Karnak. One of those obelisks is still standing today.
Then her name starts vanishing. Cartouches hacked out. Statues smashed and buried. Images plastered over. Why erase the most successful reign in a century?
Not revenge. The attacks begin near the end of her stepson's long reign, decades after her death, when any personal grudge had had a lifetime to cool.
Historians read it as paperwork. Make the crown pass straight from father to son, and the woman who reigned in between simply stops having existed.

verdicts.claim: Hatshepsut's cartouches and images were chiselled off or covered on her monuments and her statues were smashed or buried.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia states that near the end of Thutmose III's reign and into Amenhotep II's her cartouches and images were chiselled off or covered and her statues smashed or buried.

verdicts.claim: Hatshepsut ruled Egypt as pharaoh for about twenty-one years in the 15th century BC and was depicted with pharaonic regalia including the false beard.
verdicts.note: 71% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Hatshepsut's mortuary temple stands at Deir el-Bahari and she erected twin obelisks at the entrance to the Karnak temple, one of which still stands and is the second-tallest ancient standing obelisk.
verdicts.note: 95% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: The erasure of Hatshepsut's monuments began near the end of Thutmose III's reign, decades after her death, and continued into the reign of Amenhotep II.
verdicts.note: 88% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: Historians including Joyce Tyldesley and Donald Redford explain the erasure as political, presenting the royal succession as running directly from Thutmose II to Thutmose III, rather than as personal vengeance.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia cites Tyldesley on Thutmose III wanting succession to run directly from Thutmose II to himself and Redford on the erasures being political necessity rather than hatred.
